title: The gold ring (James 2:1–13)
hookLine: don't give the rich visitor the good seat and the poor one the floor
last: SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.

lines: A GOLD RING, AND SHABBY CLOTHES.
cards: Two people walk into a gathering at the same moment. One has a gold ring on his finger and fine clothes. The other is in shabby, dirty clothes.
Watch where the eyes go. Watch who gets greeted first, who gets a chair, who gets a nod toward the back. Often nobody decides to do it.
It just happens, in churches, restaurants, offices. James pictures it happening in the gatherings of early believers, so sharply you can almost hear the scrape of the chairs.

teach.h: THE GOOD SEAT, AND THE FLOOR.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment."

The greeters say to the rich man: "Sit thou here in a good place"; and to the poor man: "Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool." On the floor, by someone's feet. James calls it judging with evil thoughts.
A small detail: the Greek word for assembly here is synagogue, the ordinary word for a gathering. Some readers take it as a sign of how close these believers were to synagogue life.

teach.h: GOD CHOSE THE POOR, RICH IN FAITH.
teach.b: Then a question: "Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith?" The people sent to the floor are the ones God honors.
Then he reaches for the royal law, the king's law, from Leviticus: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Favoritism breaks it.

teach.h: THE ROYAL LAW: LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR.
teach.b: You can't love your neighbor as yourself while assigning seats by the shine of their jewelry. And a short, startling ending.
Speak and act, he says, as people who will be judged by the law of liberty, because judgment will be without mercy to anyone who has shown no mercy. And then: "mercy rejoiceth against judgment."
Modern versions say mercy triumphs over judgment.
Picture a courtroom where mercy stands up and wins.
This week has moved from Philippians into James: rejoice always, whatever is lovely, contentment, count it all joy, every good gift, quick to hear, and now the gold ring.

how: Some churches read James 2:1–9 when training greeters and welcome teams, as a check on who gets noticed at the door.

games.q: you're greeting at the door. a man with a gold ring and a man in dirty clothes arrive together. there's one good seat left. what does James say happens?
o: the poor man gets it, because he's more in need.
the rich man gets it, and the poor man is sent to the floor.
games.why: "Sit thou here in a good place" to the rich, "sit here under my footstool" to the poor. James calls it judging with evil thoughts.

practice: Picture the places you go in a normal week, a bus, a break room, a family table, and ask who usually gets the good seat, and who ends up quietly on the edge.
Let one easy-to-overlook face come to mind, and picture making room for them: a chair pulled out, a question asked, your attention turned their way. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: Synagogue. The ordinary Greek word for a gathering, the word James uses for the believers' meeting, where the rich man gets the good seat and the poor man the floor.

orig.note: Greek: a gathering, an assembly. James uses it for the believers' meeting, the same word as synagogue.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy triumphs over judgment. The one who shows mercy is met by it. A week of letters, done.
